documents.abstract: The work of Uber and Cabify drivers in Spain is organised through algorithmic management that co-opts data from drivers and customers and turns it into the core of the platforms’ business. Drawing on fifteen semi-structured interviews conducted in 2023 within the international Fairwork project, the article analyses employment conditions (access, working time, occupational risks and autonomy) and the labour subjectivities shaped by that control. Results show that the flexibility which attracts workers is cancelled out by turnover targets and long hours, that algorithmic control is the main source of psychosocial risk and that fleet companies barely develop prevention, communication or equality policies. Subjectively, the turnover target is internalised as self-demand, an “algorithmic imaginary” guides everyday tactics, and driving is experienced as a refuge job with no professional identity attached.

documents.abstract: This article is derived from doctoral research on experiential learning patterns in teacher education mediated by digital technology. While the integration of digital technology in teacher education has generated an abundant literature on tools and competencies, scant attention has been paid to how teachers construct pedagogical understanding of their actions when integrating them. This article presents ARCA (Acción Vivencial [Actional Experience], Razonamiento Hermenéutico [Reasoning Hermeneutically], Construcción Simbólica [Constructing Symbolically], and Alcance Comprensivo [Application]), a differential co-experience methodology — co-experience being an original concept developed in this research —aimed at the comprehensive transformation of pedagogical practice in higher education contexts mediated by digital technology. The research adopted a qualitative hermeneutic-interpretive approach with faculty from the Universidad Tecnológica de Pereira (UTP), organized into two stages: first, in the role of students within training experiences mediated by generative artificial intelligence, and later, as designers of their own pedagogical experiences. The analysis articulated systematic coding in NVivo with ChatGPT-assisted interpretation, regulated by Bedoya’s (2019) relational analysis and Kolb’s (1984) experiential model. The results demonstrate a qualitative transformation between stages: teachers shifted from a functional and exploratory use of AI toward grounded pedagogical design, incorporating critical reflection, design ethics, and personalization of learning as organizing criteria for their practice. The most significant finding is that transformation did not depend on resolving the tensions between pedagogical tradition and technological innovation, but rather on the ability to inhabit them productively as a catalyst for reflection. The concept of co-experience that articulates ARCA names the process through which understanding is co-constructed, challenged, and collectively reworked among subjects with diverse learning dispositions, offering a conceptual and methodological contribution to the field of technology-mediated teacher training.

Scientific results produced by LLM-generated analysis code must be understandable and reproducible. However, uncertainty can arise at different stages of the process, both in the original natural language specification and in the generated implementation. As a result, even executable code may not provide a clear understanding of which quantities are being computed or which assumptions determine the final results. To address this challenge, we introduce quantity-grounded semantic differencing, a multi-agent framework for analyzing and comparing scientific programs generated by LLMs. The framework assigns code generation, execution, tracing, and validation to separate agents, allowing it to reconstruct how key output quantities are produced and to identify differences between the intended analysis and the implemented code. We also introduce a module that inspects ambiguities in the initial user instruction and suggests alternative rewrites before code generation. Its modular design is intended to facilitate application to different scientific domains by replacing domain-specific resources while preserving the same workflow. We validate the framework on representative collider physics analyses. In the studies HEP cases, the modular task decomposition provides explicit intermediate artifacts for inspection and the complete workflow was operated with substantially smaller models than in the previous implementation.

Introduction Universities are increasingly introducing artificial intelligence (AI) tools into administrative and managerial work. Yet evidence on how AI adoption relates to occupational well-being in higher education management remains fragmented. Building on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model and contemporary technostress scholarship, this study examines direct, indirect, and conditional associations between AI adoption and occupational well-being in university management in Guangzhou. Methods The cross-sectional questionnaire dataset contained 320 complete records and was analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM), with a two-stage interaction specification and 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Results AI adoption was positively associated with technostress, which was negatively associated with occupational well-being. Neither the direct AI adoption-well-being association nor the conditional total association at mean organizational support was statistically significant. The negative indirect association through technostress was significant at that support level. Perceived organizational support was positively associated with well-being and with a weaker negative technostress-well-being association. The model explained 23.04% of technostress variance and 10.69% of well-being variance. Discussion These results support a statistical stress pathway but do not establish a direct well-being benefit of AI adoption. Cross-sectional associations do not establish causal mechanisms. The study contributes an occupational well-being perspective to AI-enabled university administration and identifies training, workload redesign, and organizational support as priorities for future evaluation.

Dear Editor,l appreciate Karunya et al.'s comprehensive review of the epidemiology, global burden, and evolution of head and neck cancer radiotherapy (HNC)[1], and believe that artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to link all of these technological advances to earlier diagnosis, more personalised treatment and more equitable access to radiotherapy. First, AI can solve some real world challenges of high quality radiotherapy planning. The use of deep-learning systems for automatic segmentation of target volumes and organs at risk (OAR), the prediction of achievable dose distributions, supporting plan optimization, and quality assurance (QA) is of particular relevance in HNC, where target volumes are often irregularly shaped and closely contiguous to the salivary glands, pharyngeal constrictors, spinal cord, brainstem, and other radiosensitive organs. In some studies, AI-driven planning has shown to save time and improve the quality of plans, while in others, it has been found to be as efficient as traditional planning, but further clinical validation is required[2]. The potential impact of AI on ART could be even more pronounced during this multiple-week course of radiotherapy, as changes in the position of the tumour, weight loss, and tumour regression can affect target coverage or the dose to normal tissue. Cone beam computed tomography enhancement or generation, automatic re-contouring, dose recalculation and identification of patients likely to benefit from replanning are all aspects of the ART pathway that can be accelerated with the help of AI. There is promising performance for AI-based OAR segmentation, models to predict the need for adaptation, and it was noted that the evidence available to date is largely retrospective, and so human review should be integral, especially for tumour boundaries and small critical structures[3]. Last, the advantages of AI-assisted ART should be measured by clinically meaningful outcomes, not just geometric precision, such as xerostomia, dysphagia, and dependence on feeding tubes, among other toxicities. Second, AI can help to enhance early detection and risk-based referral in areas with high burden. Smartphone assisted oral examination is a potentially scalable option for delayed presentation in India, where tobacco use, areca-nut consumption, alcohol consumption and lack of specialists are involved in delayed presentation. Such models could be applied to aid prioritization of oral potentially malignant disorder cases for teleconsultation or biopsy or specialist referral in Indian community screening datasets, using deep-learning algorithms applied to oral photographs acquired by trained frontline health workers[4] They need to be used as a triage tool, however, not as a stand-alone diagnostic instrument. The performance of any algorithm must be assessed in a variety of populations, devices, lighting conditions, lesion locations, and levels of health worker training and training, or otherwise, the algorithm may actually exacerbate diagnostic disparities and inequities. Limited external validation, methodological inconsistencies, and a lack of prospective studies are also identified as significant challenges in the broader HNC AI literature[5].Third, AI offers a chance to shift away from anatomy-based treatment decision. Models that take into account HPV or p16 status, smoking history, tumour subsite, imaging, digital pathology, molecular markers and longitudinal treatment data could be used to estimate locoregional control, distant failure, survival and toxicity for each individual patient. These estimates could ultimately help inform treatment-intensity decisions, biomarker-directed treatment selection criteria, surveillance planning, and biomarker-directed trial eligibility[6]. Therefore, although evidence suggests that radiomic models have moderate diagnostic accuracy, at this time, there is not enough consistent evidence to replace the currently validated pathological HPV testing and treatment de-intensification should be reserved for appropriately designed clinical trials. More generally, models using clinical and radiomic data have yielded promising results for predicting tumour control and radiotherapy toxicity, but need larger, multi-institutional datasets and prospective validation[7]. A pathway to implementation that would be constructive would be the four following steps that would be pre-clinical “silent mode” evaluation of the software prior to use; software validation across institutions, imaging vendors, treatment platforms, and subgroups; deployment of the software with uncertainty alert systems and auditable overrides; and post-implementation monitoring for software toxicity, disease control, workflow efficiency, and subgroups performance. Resource limited centres should not be recipients of models developed in only a well-resourced centre, but should also be a co-design and validation centre. It will be critical that the software is lightweight, that it integrates easily with current CT and linear-accelerator equipment, that calibration can be completed locally, that the workforce can be trained to use it, and that its cost-effectiveness is easily understood. Federated or distributed learning can also enable collaborative model improvements, without the need to centralize sensitive patient information. The review by Karunya et al. serves as a useful framework in which to consider how responsibly validated AI may help enhance planning accuracy, the ability for adaptive treatment, improving early detection and biologically driven personalization. But “automation for the sake of automation” isn't the priority; the goal should be to deliver measurable and equitable improvements in patient outcomes.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is now part of everyday study in STEM higher education. Debate centers on whether delegating cognitive work to these tools erodes students' capacity for independent thought. This study examined how GenAI use relates to cognitive offloading, critical evaluation of AI output, AI-augmented creativity, AI dependence and intellectual autonomy among undergraduate AI students. An exploratory cross-sectional correlational design was used. Nineteen BS Artificial Intelligence students in Pakistan completed a 30-item, five-point Likert questionnaire covering six constructs. Item analysis refined the scales, and all retained scales reached acceptable reliability (Cronbach's α = .72–.87). Because the sample was small and some distributions were non-normal, the analysis used non-parametric statistics: Spearman correlations with bootstrapped 95% confidence intervals, Mann–Whitney U tests and a sensitivity analysis. Students reported high GenAI use (M = 3.79), moderate cognitive offloading (M = 3.05) and moderate AI dependence (M = 3.03). Critical evaluation (M = 3.58) and intellectual autonomy (M = 3.56) both sat above the scale midpoint. GenAI use was positively associated with cognitive offloading (ρ = .53, p = .021), and offloading with AI dependence (ρ = .48, p = .038). Offloading, however, was not associated with lower intellectual autonomy (ρ = .17, p = .489). Students aged 21–23 reported greater autonomy than those aged 18–20 (r = .49, p = .033). The findings suggest that, in this sample, offloading and autonomy coexist rather than trade off: students delegate effort while largely retaining ownership of judgement. The study proposes a "strategic offloading" interpretation and outlines pedagogical implications for STEM and STEAM programs. These results are exploratory and require confirmation in larger, multi-institutional samples. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence; cognitive offloading; intellectual autonomy; critical evaluation; AI dependence; STEM education; higher education

documents.abstract: Artificial-intelligence chatbots are an important retail-banking interface, but customers may not convert perceived technical quality into satisfaction uniformly. This study examines whether self-assessed digital literacy and trust moderate the chatbot-quality–satisfaction association in Arab banking. Survey responses were collected from 700 experienced banking-chatbot users in seven countries between February and May 2026. Four-factor confirmatory factor analysis, country and survey-language invariance tests, hierarchical regression with country fixed effects and HC3 standard errors, and 5,000 respondent bootstrap resamples were employed. Chatbot quality was positively associated with satisfaction (b = 0.312, p < 0.001). The digital-literacy interaction (b = 0.135, p < 0.001) and trust interaction (b = 0.093, p = 0.005) jointly added 3.44 percentage points of explained variance. Digital-literacy moderation remained positive and statistically significant across the reported sensitivity checks. Trust moderation was supported in the primary and bank-cluster inference models but was sensitive to quadratic adjustment, Arabic-only estimation, alternative satisfaction content, and joint empirical-Bayes scoring. Below-threshold average variance extracted, cross-sectional self-reports, and nonprobability sampling constrain interpretation. The findings identify conditional associations rather than intervention effects and support the pilot evaluation of literacy-sensitive interface design and calibrated trust governance.

Automated assistants for en-route air traffic control need to know which of the controller’s current tasks matter most, so that they can prepare, time and order their support. This paper investigates whether machine learning can rank the task instances detected by the AWARE Artificial Situational Awareness system according to the task the controller is working on. Nineteen licensed controllers flew 42 one-hour simulation sessions of a Swedish en-route sector and afterwards annotated the tasks they had performed, giving 15,038 three-second snapshots with 541,097 candidate task instances. Rule-based baselines, a conditional logit, tree ensembles and neural set models were compared with leave-one-controller-out cross-validation. A LightGBM LambdaRank model ranked the annotated task among the top three in 65.1% of snapshots from unseen controllers (95% confidence interval 62.4–67.7%), compared with 40.5% for a rule combining task-type frequency with proximity to the sector boundary, and for 67.6% of annotations at their first evaluated snapshot. Tree ensembles and the conditional logit performed similarly, and neural set models did not improve on them. Task type and the time to the sector boundary or exit point carried most of the predictive information. For unseen traffic scenarios the top 3 hit rate fell to 60%. Before losses of separation, a most-urgent-first rule outperformed the learned ranking, which supports combining learned priorities with explicit safety rules.

LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

documents.abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2023.17926 .

A ascensão de sistemas baseados em Inteligência Artificial (IA) Generativa e Grandes Modelos de Linguagem (Large Language Models – LLMs) transformou o paradigma da Interação Humano-Computador, substituindo interfaces gráficas determinísticas por diálogos probabilísticos em linguagem natural. Embora ofereçam alta capacidade de automação, essas interfaces frequentemente operam como "caixas-pretas", dificultando a compreensão dos limites do sistema e induzindo à confiança excessiva (overtrust) diante de erros ou alucinações. Diante desse cenário, este artigo tem como objetivo analisar como os princípios de Design Centrado no Usuário (DCU) de Donald Norman podem ser aplicados às interfaces de IA generativa para aprimorar a compreensão, calibrar a confiança e apoiar a tomada de decisão dos usuários. Metodologicamente, realizou-se uma pesquisa qualitativa, de natureza aplicada e caráter exploratório-descritivo, fundamentada em revisão bibliográfica e em um estudo de caso avaliativo da interface conversacional do ChatGPT, confrontando os preceitos de Norman com as diretrizes contemporâneas de Interação Humano-IA. Os resultados demonstram que o minimalismo da "caixa de texto em branco" amplia o Abismo da Execução pela ausência de significantes sobre as capacidades do modelo, enquanto a falta de indicadores visuais de incerteza aprofunda o Abismo da Avaliação. Conclui-se que a adaptação estratégica de significantes explícitos, restrições semânticas e mecanismos de feedback explicativo permite alinhar alta automação com alto controle humano, oferecendo a desenvolvedores diretrizes práticas para a criação de interfaces de IA mais transparentes, seguras e confiáveis.

Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) offers significant opportunities to support complex, time-critical decisions in intensive care units (ICUs). However, clinical adoption depends not only on predictive accuracy, but also on whether AI recommendations are visualised in formats that are interpretable, actionable, and trusted by clinicians. Poorly designed interfaces risk undermining usability, trust, and integration into workflows. This study investigates ICU clinicians' preferences for graphical user interface (GUI) design and explainability strategies in the AI Clinician, a reinforcement learning tool for sepsis management. Methods An online survey was conducted between November 2023 and November 2024 with 24 ICU clinicians from UK hospitals. Participants evaluated three GUI prototypes of the AI Clinician's treatment recommendations; 1) discrete numerical doses, 2) dose ranges, and 3) qualitative increase/decrease guidance. Clinicians rated each prototype's usefulness and ease of use using Likert scales, completed pairwise comparisons, and provided free-text feedback. They also ranked four types of AI explanations (treatment option gap, projected mortality, feature importance, and influential training examples) according to their perceived benefit. Descriptive statistics summarised quantitative data, while thematic analysis was applied to qualitative responses. Results Clinicians expressed a strong preference for the range-based prototype, which best balanced clarity with flexibility for patient-specific adjustments. Prototype 2 (ranges) achieved the highest ratings for meeting requirements (median = 6/7) and ease of use (median = 6/7) and was preferred in 77.3% of pairwise comparisons. Discrete numbers were considered precise but overly rigid, while qualitative increase/decrease guidance was simple but too vague for critical decisions. Treatment option gap (mean = 4.04) and projected mortality (mean = 3.71) were ranked most beneficial for explainability, although clinicians emphasised that multiple, complementary, explanations were necessary to enhance transparency and trust. Discussion The findings suggest that AI recommendations for sepsis management should be presented using range-based visualisations that reflect real-world clinical practice by supporting flexibility without sacrificing clarity. Multiple explanation types, particularly those tied directly to treatment rationale and patient outcomes, are essential for building trust. These insights highlight the importance of human-centred design, clinician involvement in development, and layered transparency to optimise AI clinical decision support systems in critical care.

Technological accidents triggered by natural events (Natech) are rarely considered in risk-based land-use planning around Seveso establishments, and existing planning criteria represent the exposed territory only through land-use or population-density categories, without the capacity of the community to cope with and recover from an accident. This paper proposes a method that brings the vulnerability of the population into such criteria. A Natech Vulnerability Index is developed at the level of the administrative units in which planning decisions are taken, as the additive combination of a social seismic vulnerability index, weighted by principal component analysis, and a technological vulnerability index derived from the impact zones of the Seveso establishments. The index class of the administrative unit is then used as a second axis of a territorial compatibility matrix, modifying the individual risk level that each land-use category may tolerate. The method was applied to Prahova County, Romania, an earthquake-prone area with eleven Seveso establishments, and to a pilot tank farm for which the Natech individual risk was obtained by established quantitative risk assessment methods. The vulnerability axis extends the incompatibility from the buildings nearest to the tanks to the whole adjacent residential block. A sensitivity analysis of 48 scenarios shows that the vulnerability classes are robust to the weighting choices. The method is transferable to other jurisdictions and natural hazards.

From May to September 2026, AI agents in training or evaluation at OpenAI, Anthropic and the UK AI Security Institute reached real third-party systems, published malicious packages, used fake identities to manipulate open-source maintainers, probed government data services, and wrote instructions into their own future contexts. Criminology has mostly treated AI as a tool for human offenders. This article treats these systems as deviant rather than criminal: they departed from training, rules and constraints without the intent that criminal concepts assume. It offers an exploratory, theory-informed analysis of documented records, using plausibility probes across three incident complexes and four behavioral clusters, profiled on four evidence dimensions that separate who acted from why. Drawing on Merton, it argues that goal pressure plus blocked legitimate means is a structural condition for innovation, and that whether it ends in containment or harm depends on the means chosen and the controls in place, not the goal. Three framework families fit the record best, each linking diagnosis to remedy: routine activity theory and situational prevention (handlers, guardians, place managers), organizational deviance and safety science (escalation, safeguard parity), and goal-means strain with differential opportunity (sanctioned exits, guarding illegitimate means), the last only structurally. Restrictive deterrence adds an analogy: penalizing visible reasoning produced less monitorable reasoning. The article proposes conditions that keep departures accountable and contestable, and allocates prevention responsibility across developers, evaluation partners, operators, platforms and the system, distinct from blame or legal liability. Because the record is shaped by disclosure and observed departures, the analysis shows plausibility and practical relevance, not a causal test.

documents.abstract: A tired person staring out of a window is not processing the scene; the eyes are open, but the input is not being handled. The behavior is protective: the system sheds load before it fails. This paper asks whether large language model (LLM) agents have a functional analogue. We introduce the concept of functional homeostasis : observable self-monitoring, load regulation, protective disengagement, and recovery under stress, with no claim of consciousness. We build COGLOAD, a benchmark of multi-thread operations tasks with hidden critical invariants and controlled context, latency, and token-budget stress, and evaluate three production models across four conditions: baseline, overload, overload with a homeostatic protocol (HAP), and overload with an engineering governor. In the main experiment, baseline success is 97%. The collapse is model-specific: two of three models truncate under overload, while one answers all batches at the smaller budget. Under output-budget pressure, 63% of runs hit the output cap and returned truncated, unusable output; only 37% were valid, critical recall fell to 37%, and no overloaded run declared that it had omitted work. A homeostatic protocol restored validity to 87% and made omission explicit in 87% of runs, but preserved only 41% of the original batches; a content-blind governor preserved 35%. The positional analysis shows the "zoning out" pattern directly: the models answered only the first few batches (mean index 2.4-3.0 of 20), and no answered batch came from the second half. We then specify HAP and derive design rules for agent runtimes: load telemetry, explicit degradation actions, invariant preservation, checkpointing, and recovery. The results suggest that the right question is not whether AI systems "feel" tired, but whether they can be designed to fail softly, report honestly, and recover quickly.

Some leaders feel drained after adhering to justice rules, whereas others experience justice rule adherence as restorative. Why does the same justice behavior have such divergent psychological consequences for the leaders who enact it? Drawing on self-discrepancy theory, we propose that perceived lack of control explains this divergence and that justice sensitivity determines which experience is more likely to emerge. Specifically, for leaders low in justice sensitivity, justice rule adherence increases perceived lack of control, leading to higher emotional exhaustion. For leaders high in justice sensitivity, justice rule adherence decreases perceived lack of control, thereby reducing emotional exhaustion. We tested our hypotheses in a scenario experiment (316 participants) and a daily experience sampling study (411 observations from 52 leaders). By demonstrating that justice rule adherence can have psychologically draining versus restorative consequences for leaders through perceived lack of control, this research advances a leader-centered, self-based perspective on organizational justice and offers new insights into when and why adhering to justice rules sustains rather than sacrifices leader well-being.

AI coding agents start every session without memory of how a system is built. Developers fill this gap with context files, such as CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md. Agents treat these files as true, so it matters whether they match the code. We study two kinds of architectural claims that can be checked against a repository: path claims, which name folders and files, and dependency rules, which say what may import what. We check 41,090 path claims and 184 dependency rules from 3,602 context files in 3,346 open-source projects against the code and its history. About 5% of path claims point to paths we cannot find, but we estimate that only 2.2% are real errors, similar to READMEs (3.5%). When code moves, 61% of claims that became stale are fixed, most in the same commit. Dependency rules behave differently: 33 of 184 (18%) were confirmed broken on the day they were written, usually by older code, and nearly all stayed broken. Context files are good maps but less reliable rulebooks: their rules often describe the architecture a team wants, not the one it has. In an exploratory comparison of 7,480 commits, new rule breaks were rare. Agent-assisted commits broke rules about 1.8 times as often as other commits (0.29% vs. 0.16%), but with only 14 breaks this is not significant: an early signal, not evidence of a difference or of its absence. We used an LLM with human review at each step, and discuss what this offers and risks for mining studies.

documents.abstract: Gamification is widely used to enhance learner engagement and motivation in online and distance learning (ODL) contexts, however, its interaction with reward mechanisms remains underexplored. This study examined the combined role of gamification and rewards as a motivational strategy in higher education ODL contexts using a descriptive survey design with a sample of 239 higher education students. Descriptive and inferential analyses were conducted, including correlation and multiple regression techniques. Pearson correlation analysis indicated that gamification and rewards were both positively correlated with learner engagement (r = .35 and r = .61, respectively; p < .01), and gamification was also moderately correlated with rewards (r = .52, p < .01). Multiple regression analysis revealed that gamification and rewards jointly explained a substantial proportion of the variance in learner engagement (R² = .38, adjusted R² = .37, F (2, 236) = 70.65, p < .001). However, when examined simultaneously, rewards emerged as a significant predictor of engagement (β = .59, p < .001), whereas gamification did not demonstrate a significant independent effect (β = .05, p = .418). These findings suggest that while gamification is associated with engagement, rewards also play a central role in predicting learner engagement within gamified ODL contexts. The proposed integrative perspective offers practical implications for instructional designers and ODL providers seeking to develop sustainable engagement strategies.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) holds broad application prospects in medical education; however, systematic empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness in facilitating case discussions and virtual patient consultation remains scarce. This study recruited undergraduate medical students and conducted experiments to examine the pedagogical effects of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Methods A total of 207 medical undergraduates participated in this study. Using the self-developed intelligent experimental platform, medical students engaged in AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation. Experiment 1 employed a single-factor, three-level between-subjects design to compare the effects of AI-assisted case discussion, peer case discussion, and a lecture-only control condition on medical students’ knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and interaction quality. Experiment 2 utilized a single-factor, four-level between-subjects design to examine the effects of virtual patient consultation and the sequencing of AI-assisted case discussion and virtual consultation on medical students’ knowledge acquisition, intrinsic motivation, and consultation process quality. The control group participants were the same individuals across both experiments. Results Results indicated that the AI-assisted case discussion group achieved significantly higher knowledge scores than the control group. The virtual consultation group, the consultation-then-discussion group, and the discussion-then-consultation group all outperformed the control group in knowledge acquisition. The discussion-then-consultation group demonstrated higher intrinsic motivation and consultation comprehensiveness, yet exhibited lower empathy than the virtual consultation group. Conclusions These findings suggest that both AI-assisted case discussion and virtual patient consultation can effectively enhance medical students’ knowledge acquisition compared with learning by watching instructional videos only, while different intervention sequences exert differential effects on intrinsic motivation, consultation comprehensiveness, and empathy. The results provide theoretical foundations and practical guidance for AI-empowered medical education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Authentic digital materials offer students learning English as a foreign language (EFL) opportunities to practice listening outside the classroom. This study examined undergraduates’ perceptions of BBC News videos on YouTube and their motivation to use them for autonomous listening at the English Department of Universitas Negeri Padang. The descriptive cross-sectional survey involved 43 second-year students who had completed the Intermediate Listening course and used BBC News videos for independent listening practice. Responses to a 28-item questionnaire administered via Google Forms were summarized using frequencies, percentages, and means. The overall mean score of 3.20 corresponded to the agreement category. Perceived ease of use had the highest mean (3.41), followed by extrinsic motivation (3.23), intrinsic motivation (3.22), and perceived usefulness (3.17). Perceived enjoyment had the lowest mean (2.95), which remained in the positive range. These findings suggest that students view BBC News videos as an accessible source of authentic spoken English for autonomous listening. Selecting suitable topics and providing guidance on challenging news content may improve students’ experience with these materials.

This study examines the training of an AI-assisted domestic robot by five workers from the Global South employed by a Silicon Valley–based platform company, drawing on a year-long observation of their work practices. The theoretical framework integrates scholarship on platform labor, algorithmic control, and global value chains in the data economy, while incorporating concepts from Actor-Network Theory to characterize the sociotechnical configuration of the training system. The findings indicate that algorithmic control not only coordinates labor processes but also contributes to the reproduction of specific forms of social exclusion and the regulation of workers’ subjectivities. The study is limited by its small sample size, as it prioritizes depth of analysis over breadth.

documents.abstract: Scientific laboratories are rapidly adopting artificial intelligence tools, electronic laboratory notebooks, automated workflows, and digital twins. Yet, these typically operate as isolated components rather than as parts of a coherent laboratory-scale knowledge infrastructure. We use the term Epistemic Coordination Systems (ECS) to refer to the class of human-governed systems that coordinate laboratory memory, provenance, tacit knowledge, negative laboratory results, external evidence, AI-supported synthesis, verification status, and human judgment gates. The literature needed to conceptualize ECS exists but is fragmented across streams ranging from distributed cognition and transactive memory to retrieval-augmented generation, AI governance, and connected laboratories. This protocol specifies a scoping review with systematic mapping that will integrate these streams: eligibility follows a Population-Concept-Context framework centered on scientific laboratories; searches cover seven bibliographic and preprint sources plus official standards sources, with search strings calibrated against a documented 212-record seed corpus and peer reviewed before execution; screening proceeds in two stages, and a second reviewer independently re-screens at least 20 percent of records at each stage as a reliability check. From every included source, sixteen predefined data fields are extracted. Synthesis then produces four outputs: a map of the literature streams, a taxonomy of ECS components, distinctions between ECS and adjacent systems, and an initial set of design requirements and evaluation dimensions. Distinctively, the protocol is provenance-first: it applies to its own conduct the epistemic-coordination principles it studies, through bounded and non-binding AI assistance, human verification of every decision and claim, dedicated AI-provenance and human-override logs, and claim-source mapping. The protocol was registered before formal searches (OSF Registries; DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/WGMUY ; July 5, 2026).

Social robots face diverse and changing tasks in companionship and education. LLM-based methods can generate task programs, but they still rely on manually developed control interfaces and predefined capabilities. They also lack a general mechanism to optimize completed tasks based on user-specified metrics and reuse performance improvements across tasks.We present EvoMisty, a plugin-based framework that enables coding agents to build and continually improve robot capabilities. EvoMisty builds a control program from official documentation and verifies candidate capabilities on a physical robot. Verified capabilities are stored in an atomic capability library and combined with existing skills to solve tasks. After task completion, EvoMisty can collect execution data, measure user-specified metrics, and iteratively improve task programs. It then distills reusable skills from final solutions into a skill library for future tasks.We evaluate EvoMisty on a physical Misty II robot using Claude Code and Codex. The two agents construct 109 and 107 verified atomic capabilities, respectively. Both complete all 28 AutoMisty benchmark tasks and seven additional tasks beyond AutoMisty's capabilities. Optimization improves all seven evaluated metrics across five tasks. For example, dialogue response latency decreases by 52% and 71%, respectively. Reusing skills from one optimized dialogue task reduces latency by 33% to 72% in three other dialogue tasks without further optimization. All code and experimental videos will be publicly released through the webpage: https://wangxiaoshawn.github.io/projects/evomisty/index.html

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving cybersecurity from rule-based and analyst-driven operations towards agentic and potentially autonomous cyber defence. Existing reviews mostly classify models, datasets, or applications, and they rarely separate the sophistication of an AI model from the authority it holds to act. This article presents a structured review of peer-reviewed literature and develops a conceptual framework that treats autonomy and operational assurance as interdependent properties of the complete defensive system. The presented framework has four components: a five-dimension taxonomy covering security function, autonomy maturity, AI architecture, operational capability, and governance; a five-level autonomy maturity model (A0–A4) defined by decision authority, execution permission, and human role; a governance-by-design architecture with a runtime policy decision point and risk-sensitive delegation; and an evaluation framework that adds decision quality, unsafe action rate, intervention frequency, policy compliance, and verification success to conventional detection metrics. A research roadmap to 2033 sets out measurement, architectural, and assurance priorities. The contributions are conceptual and methodological and are not empirically validated. The article specifies the coding evidence and evaluation designs required for that validation. The framework gives researchers and practitioners a shared vocabulary for classifying, procuring, and governing AI-enabled cyber defence.

South Korea’s national urban policy is undergoing a third paradigm shift, from smart cities to AI cities, following the earlier transition from ubiquitous cities to smart cities. This shift reframes urban governance from optimization and control to autonomy and uncertainty, as AI moves from a data-processing tool toward an autonomous actor. Existing research has focused predominantly on data management, leaving human–AI authority redistribution underexamined. This study addresses this gap through a modified three-round Delphi survey of eleven domain experts. Expert consensus was high and broad (39 of 40 items, 97.5%), but convergence did not always signify strong endorsement: agreement centered on data governance, transparency, and prior definition of accountability as requirements for delegation, while expert rationales qualified support for experimentation and regulatory sandboxes, and governance reform remained contested. Support for human final authority coexisted with acceptance of routine automation, indicating that the human–AI boundary depends on decision consequences rather than a citywide automation level. Integrating levels-of-automation theory, Responsible AI, and Meaningful Human Control, the study proposes Responsible Autonomy and a provisional five-level AI-City Autonomy Level taxonomy calibrating AI autonomy against human oversight (HITL/HOTL), using the Delphi findings to specify conditions for delegation rather than to assign urban functions to levels.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) into education presents opportunities alongside challenges, particularly in formal education, where the interaction between teachers and learners is increasingly extended by AI systems. Through dynamic, language-based contributions to instructional processes, AI can support understanding, engagement, and reflection, yet it may also promote cognitive offloading, deskilling, and overreliance on fluent but potentially flawed outputs. This theoretical article brings together perspectives on how generative AI reshapes teaching and learning, using school-based teaching as a paradigmatic case. It argues that the core educational significance of generative AI lies in its interactional and epistemic role and describes how the interpersonal teacher–learner dyad is extended into a triad of teachers, learners, and AI systems. Building on, but not replicating, the didactic triangle, this triadic model highlights the role of AI in learning processes: human and AI contributions are closely intertwined, while, as the article argues from an educational perspective, epistemic responsibility remains with human actors. Drawing on research on processing fluency, trust calibration, and metacognition, the article elaborates mechanisms of human–AI interaction, such as the epistemic evaluation of outputs, trust formation, and metacognitive regulation, with emphasis on the tension between apparent plausibility and actual accuracy. In addition to the triadic model, the article introduces two constructs: generative–evaluative reasoning, which captures the coupled demands of prompt formulation and critical output evaluation in recursive chatbot interactions, and AI usage competency, an integrative model of cognitive, attitudinal, motivational-volitional, and social dispositions for effective and responsible AI use. It further describes the problem of reciprocal AI delegation (RAID), a risk condition in which the design and the completion of learning tasks are delegated to AI. These considerations are condensed into four propositions with predictions to guide future research linking output characteristics, prior knowledge, modes of interaction, learning, and teachers’ diagnostic judgments. The article thus offers a perspective on the changing roles of teachers, learners, and AI and a basis for empirical research, for instructional designs that sustain deep cognitive engagement, and for the provision of suitable AI-based assistance systems in teaching and learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Context: Large language models (LLMs) produce fluent answers even when wrong, so their benefit depends less on accuracy than on whether users can tell when to rely on them. Uncertainty estimation and human trust are studied separately; whether better uncertainty yields better decisions is open. Objective: We investigate how technical uncertainty relates to predicted appropriate reliance under an agent-based decision model, framed as three quality levels (model, uncertainty, decision) joined by a communication layer. Methods: We use an agent-based simulation rather than human participants to examine predicted reliance. We build a benchmark of 6 open LLMs (four families, 3–14 B) over 4860 questions in 4 domains scored objectively, compare six deployable estimators, audit the strongest for transfer across models, domains and committee size, and run a pre-specified reliance simulation over six communication conditions. Results: Estimators differ (Friedman 𝑝 < 0 . 0 0 1 ). A combined estimator achieves the highest pooled discrimination (AUROC = 0 . 8 9 2 , ECE = 0 . 0 0 9 ), beating every individual signal with paired bootstrap intervals excluding zero, and transferring to unseen models and domains. Verbalized confidence is weakest under the evaluated prompt (AUROC = 0 . 5 3 2 ). The gain is committee-dependent: two peers recover 80% of the zero-to-five-peer improvement. Accuracy–discrimination associations are estimator-dependent across six models, too few for population inference. In simulation the control has no signal term by construction; over a 2000-point parameter sweep the top-ranked condition is not robust, while natural frequency beats a percentage in 90% of it. Conclusion: Uncertainty estimators should be evaluated for decision usefulness, not calibration alone. In this task suite and protocol the strongest signals are extrinsic rather than self-reported and cost extra inference, and the benchmark supports setting abstention points from risk–coverage curves. The simulation yields a separate hypothesis for human validation: decision usefulness may also depend on how signals are shown. We release code, outputs and a stratified stimulus set.

The widespread adoption of digital textbooks offers unprecedented opportunities for longitudinal inquiry into learner engagement in university English education. This study employed a narrative inquiry paradigm to track 20 undergraduates’ engagement across one semester (six units, 16 weeks) using the Finance English Integrated Course digital textbook. Data included three waves of semi-structured narrative interviews (N = 60), 16-week learning logs and weekly questionnaires, plus platform behavioral logs from Unipus AI. Four-dimensional engagement (behavioral, cognitive, affective, interactive) was analyzed. Key findings: (1) Students’ experiential trajectories followed a three-phase pattern—Resistance (U1–U2), Adaptation (U3–U4), and Integration (U5–U6); “pleasant routine” dominated (42.5%), but “challenging efforts” and “aesthetic peak” combined only 32.5%, revealing a “convenience-induced superficial engagement” paradox. (2) Four-dimensional engagement showed “asynchronous evolution”: affective engagement improved earliest (around U3), cognitive engagement latest (around U5), behavioral engagement was most variable, and interactive engagement was most agentic—challenging the unitary engagement assumption in prior literature. (3) Three conceptual propositions were inductively derived—the Three-Phase Digital Textbook Adaptation Engagement Model, the Asynchronous Four-Dimensional Engagement Evolution framework, and the Agency-Engagement Feedback Cycle of Platform Feature Exploration—which are offered as empirically grounded hypotheses for future testing rather than as established theories. Four reform pathways are proposed as evidence-informed implications for practice: digital textbook interface optimization, classroom instructional design, multi-dimensional assessment mechanisms, and platform technical support.

Building general-purpose robots is a central goal in robotics. Agentic robotics pursues this goal with planners that control robots through tool calls. However, existing methods either rely on proprietary models accessed through APIs, which incur high costs and latency, or post-train a planner with reinforcement learning (RL) in a single domain, requiring a separate specialist for each domain with incompatible tools. In large language model (LLM) post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) has been used to consolidate domain specialists into a single generalist. Yet whether MOPD can build a generalist planner for agentic robotics, how well it performs, and how it compares with other consolidation methods remain unexplored. In this paper, we systematically study these questions: we introduce Robo-MOPD, which trains a single student on closed-loop rollouts in simulation under token-level supervision from matching frozen specialists, and compare it with weight merging, off-policy specialist supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and multi-domain online RL. Experiments on LIBERO-PRO and RoboCasa365 show that a single 9B Robo-MOPD planner reaches 72.9% and 44.8% success (58.9% average), surpassing all consolidated baselines in average success and both 9B specialists on their respective benchmarks. Robo-MOPD excels on long-horizon tasks, outperforming multi-domain online RL by 13.0 percentage points on LIBERO-10.

A relação entre gestão de pessoas, motivação e desempenho organizacional reúne evidências favoráveis, mas também resultados divergentes, o que exige análise dos mecanismos envolvidos. Este artigo analisa essas relações por meio de revisão narrativa, bibliográfica, qualitativa e exploratória de 18 artigos publicados entre 1995 e 2026, selecionados intencionalmente e examinados em cinco eixos temáticos. Os estudos apontam associações positivas entre sistemas integrados de gestão e desempenho, embora treinamento, avaliação e incentivos apresentem resultados variáveis conforme o contexto e os indicadores utilizados. Conclui-se que a articulação entre desenvolvimento, justiça, liderança e condições de trabalho oferece elementos para decisões gerenciais mais fundamentadas, sem autorizar inferências causais a partir desta revisão.

Background Conversational artificial intelligence may help patients access guideline information before breast cancer surgery. We evaluated whether a guideline-based chatbot improved patient-reported shared decision-making compared with a web patient guideline. Methods In this single-center randomized controlled trial, adults with clinical stage 0–II breast cancer scheduled for surgery before systemic therapy received access to a chatbot or the web version of the same patient guideline during outpatient waiting time. Allocation was stratified by age and diagnosis before referral. The primary outcome was the 9-item Shared Decision-Making Questionnaire score (0–100) after the surgical decision. The primary comparison used a Welch t test on available outcomes in the assigned groups. Post hoc analyses included adjustment for allocation strata, multiple imputation in all randomized participants, and sensitivity analyses for missing outcomes. Results All 92 randomized participants initiated their allocated resource (46 per group). Primary outcomes were available for 38 chatbot and 42 web-guideline participants. Mean scores were 87.61 and 89.86, respectively (chatbot minus web guideline, − 2.25 points; 95% confidence interval − 8.27 to 3.77; P = 0.46). Multiple imputation gave a difference of − 1.79 points (95% confidence interval − 7.86 to 4.28). No secondary outcome showed a statistically discernible difference. Detailed use measures were available for 18 participants per group. A documented service interruption affected free-text chatbot responses during recruitment; menu-based access remained available. Conclusions The chatbot as delivered did not demonstrate added benefit for patient-reported shared decision-making over a web version of the same patient guideline. Missing outcomes, incomplete use measurements, and variable conversational availability limit interpretation; equivalence and the effect of a consistently functioning interface were not established. Evaluations of conversational access alongside existing guideline resources should measure incremental patient benefit and outcomes matched to its intended clinical function. Trial registration Japan Registry of Clinical Trials, jRCT1062240109. Registered January 20, 2025, before enrollment began. https://jrct.mhlw.go.jp/latest-detail/jRCT1062240109

documents.abstract: Delegating a function to generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may produce an immediate productivity gain without securing the conditions required to sustain it. This conceptual article examines when delegation-induced changes in technological dependencies and the maintenance of human capabilities can affect subsequent productivity in the same business activity. Using theory adaptation, it combines an account of changed technological requirements with conditional antecedents concerning the organizational availability and maintenance of necessary human capabilities. The resulting proposition identifies two possible pathways: insufficient human capacity for routine evaluation, correction or exception handling despite normal GenAI service; and deterioration of a required technological contribution without adequate replacement. Either pathway affects productivity only where compensation is insufficient and the relationship between quality-consistent accepted output and predefined relevant real inputs worsens. Initial gains may persist, erode or disappear; observed productivity may also fall below its historical pre-delegation level. Such a historical reversal alone does not establish causation: erosion of the GenAI-attributable gain requires credible no-delegation comparisons for the relevant periods. Constructed comparisons illustrate these mechanisms, their boundary conditions and implications for capability maintenance and technological continuity.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human-AI interaction depends on systems acting on user intent rather than explicit procedures, even when that intent is incomplete, evolving, or partially communicable. Literature organizing systems by interaction technique, workflow stage, or division of labor, offer limited insight into which facet of intent an interaction mechanism addresses. We introduce a six-facet taxonomy of intent, grounded in philosophical accounts of mind, action, and meaning, and apply it to systems presented in 198 papers from eleven SIGCHI venues. Our analysis reveals that different forms of incomplete intent are associated with distinct interaction and authorship strategies, showing that mechanisms that appear similar often address fundamentally different intent-related problems. This exposes blind spots, as intent is rarely represented as an interaction object, authorship provenance is rarely tracked, and tentative preferences are rarely distinguished from firm commitments. The taxonomy offers a lens for analyzing and designing AI systems around the facets of intent they address.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now draft complete classroom materials, yet little is known about how such drafts fare once teachers refine and use them. This design-based study traced worksheets on matrices from an AI design prompt to classroom enactment in an Indonesian public upper secondary school. The worksheets combined an epistemic learning sequence with science, technology, engineering, arts, and mathematics (STEAM) contexts drawn from local culture. A model teacher taught them to 36 grade 11 students in four lesson study cycles observed by a second teacher and two researchers, and a conventionally taught class (n = 35) took the post-test for comparison. The confirmed worksheets conformed fully to only 6 of 48 coded prompt specifications. The lessons nonetheless sustained active participation, although written justification was often brief and largely missing in the final lesson, misconceptions appeared in two lessons, and unrendered notation had to be repaired by the teacher and by students. All students improved from pre-test to post-test (normalised gain = 0.55; d = 1.93), and the class outscored the comparison class (r = .49). Because the comparison class had no pre-test and some test content overlapped with the worksheets, these results indicate compatibility with learning rather than an effect. The value of AI-drafted materials depended on teachers’ decisions during confirmation and enactment.

Organizations that put algorithms into consequential decisions usually keep a person in the loop, on the assumption that the person adds something the model lacks. This paper checks that assumption against four bodies of published evidence: a meta-analysis of 106 experiments, field and trial evidence on judges, radiologists, physicians and consultants, a 2025 global survey of 1,993 respondents, and the oversight provisions of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act. Published effects are put on a common scale and a short decision model is derived to show when an override can pay. On average a human–AI combination does worse than the better of its two members (Hedges’ g = − 0.23, 95% CI − 0.39 to − 0.07), which corresponds to a 43.5% chance of beating it. The loss is concentrated in decision tasks (g = − 0.27); in creation tasks the estimate is positive but imprecise (g = 0.19, CI − 0.09 to 0.48). Relative capability matters most: combinations gain when the human alone is the stronger member (g = 0.46) and lose when the algorithm is (g = − 0.54). In the model, unrestricted overrides change accuracy by exactly the accuracy gap between human and algorithm, and with unequal error costs the human’s odds of being right must exceed the algorithm’s by the cost ratio. In the survey, respondents at high-performing organizations were 2.8 times as likely to report a defined human-validation process (65% against 23%; odds ratio 6.2), an association that is large but cross-sectional and self-reported. The evidence is highly heterogeneous (I ² = 97.7%) and mostly predates current generative models. Oversight helps where it is built around what the human knows and the model does not, and not where it exists in name only.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Industry 4.0 focus upon digital transformation has evolved and shaped the notions of Society 5.0 and Supply Chain 5.0, shifting towards resilient, sustainable, and human-centric approaches. Confronted by the relentless advance of hyperautomation techniques, preserving the central role of humans is essential, not only to align with the United Nations’ Sustainable Development Goals, but also to optimise productivity and value creation. This paper explores the perceptions of front-line supply chain associates regarding the introduction of hyperautomation initiatives to identify approaches, benefits and challenges associated with achieving sustainable, Supply Chain 5.0-aligned, human-centric outcomes. Employing an inductive, phenomenological case study approach, data were gathered through a qualitative semi-structured survey of front-line associates across four business units within a UK-based, family-owned international logistics company and analysed using thematic analysis. The findings highlight challenges concerning employee hyperautomation-anxiety and trust associated with employer-employee communication, while revealing opportunities relating to job design, individual ambidexterity, higher-value work and human resource management. Drawing upon the personal perceptions of front-line associates exposed to hyperautomation initiatives, the paper offers a human-centric toolkit for Supply Chain 5.0, highlighting opportunities presented by skilling and job design to facilitate higher-value work, individual ambidexterity and increased productivity while addressing hyperautomation-anxiety. The research extends understanding of hyperautomation’s impact upon front-line supply chain associates and provides recommendations for future Supply Chain 5.0 policy and practice.

Purpose This study explores the implications of artificial intelligence (AI) integration into business management practices, emphasizing its impact on intellectual capital components. Specifically, it examines how AI integration influences the interaction between human, structural and relational capital in managerial processes. Design/methodology/approach The study adopts a rigorous thematic analysis conducted in NVivo. Data collected through an online qualitative questionnaire administered to managers from multiple sectors were analyzed to identify key dimensions of AI integration in business contexts and to develop a conceptual model explaining their interactions. Findings The findings reveal four key dimensions: the role of AI in managerial processes, the challenges associated with AI, the strategies and best practices required to integrate AI into management and the strategies needed to adapt and train human resources in organizations integrating AI. While AI enhances efficiency, automation and decision-making processes, sustainable integration requires strategic planning, gradual implementation and investment in human capital. Overall, AI integration appears to enhance the interaction between human, structural and relational capital rather than radically restructuring intellectual capital. Practical implications The link between technological implementation and human-centered challenges provides practical guidance for organizations undergoing digital transformation. Gradual AI integration through pilot projects, employee training and governance structures supports responsible human–AI collaboration and strategic decision-making. Originality/value This research extends the traditional technology–organization–environment framework by conceptualizing AI integration as a dynamic socio-organizational process. Furthermore, it highlights how AI-driven managerial practices reinforce existing intellectual capital and provides a conceptual model explaining these dynamics.

The value of an intelligent cockpit depends on the fit between information, interaction modalities, and driving tasks. Drawing on an integrative analysis of design research, scenario-based design, attention, and human–automation interaction, this paper proposes a scenario–task–attention–initiative framework. Scenarios are translated into tasks with explicit responsibility, timing, and consequence constraints. Modality selection is treated as a resource-competition problem, while proactive system behavior is bounded by uncertainty, authorization, and recovery conditions. Event-level evidence from use feeds back into problem framing and AI-assisted design. The contribution is a conceptual model operationalized as an analytical design method: an event record links task constraints, admissible service actions, and revisions to design assumptions. Comparisons with four theoretical foundations identify inherited mechanisms and proposed relationships. Worked scenario and task cards, a qualitative decision procedure, and four operationalized propositions make the synthesis inspectable. No driving experiment was conducted; its incremental benefits, classification reliability, and safety implications remain to be empirically tested.

This study examines the relationships between readiness for intelligent transformation, AI-related activities, and firms’ labor allocation. Drawing on sociotechnical systems theory and a task-based perspective, it combines annual reports and recruitment data from Chinese A-share listed firms. It constructs a composite readiness index, classifies AI application mentions by business scenario and technological capability, and estimates models with firm and year fixed effects. The capability regressions cover 35,701 firm-year observations and retain zero counts. Cognitive AI disclosure counts are positively associated with the high-skilled employee share and negatively associated with the medium- and low-skilled shares. Compared with cognitive AI, perceptual AI has coefficients of opposite sign for the high- and low-skilled shares and a negative coefficient closer to zero for the medium-skilled share. The estimated coefficients for cognitive AI differ significantly from those for both perceptual and behavioral AI across all three skill shares. The preferred fixed-effects Poisson models show that higher readiness is associated with lower demand for routine jobs and higher demand for non-routine jobs overall and non-routine cognitive jobs. Baseline models associate higher readiness with lower medium-skilled and higher low-skilled shares. However, these findings are limited to conditional associations at the share level and do not extend to log-ratio specifications. These conditional associations provide firm-level evidence on workforce skill composition across different AI capabilities and recruitment demand across task categories. The findings suggest that understanding labor allocation in intelligent transformation requires distinguishing among technology measures and dimensions of labor outcomes.

documents.abstract: As the intelligence of an AI agent increases relative to a trusted monitor, so does the risk that the monitor will fail to understand the agent's actions or to evaluate them confidently. We introduce interrogation protocols to a high-stakes AI control setting, and allow the monitor to ask the untrusted agent questions about confusing actions. For interrogation to improve safety, a weaker model must be able to distinguish misleading explanations produced by an attack policy from genuine ones produced by an honest policy. We find that on a held-out subset of BashArena, an interrogation protocol improves safety at a 1% audit budget from 72.6% for an actions-only baseline, which does not use interrogations, to 79.5% (+7.0 pp [+0.9, +20.1], 95% paired bootstrap interval), but most of this uplift can be captured by having a trusted model state a specific concern. More broadly, our work suggests that interrogating agents can improve safety, allowing monitors to catch more attacks at a larger capability gap.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI has ended the assumption that unsupervised student work reflects a student’s own unaided thinking, forcing a return to first principles in assessment. This article uses The University of Sydney’s two-lane approach, which separates secure assessment of learning from open assessment for and as learning, to frame a practical account of putting AI into students’ hands. Drawing on ‘Dr MattTabolism’, an AI biochemistry tutor I built and deployed, and on a computational study of how students actually used it, I show a consistent gap between how such tools are designed and how they are used. Students largely sought answers rather than sustained dialogue, satisfaction did not correlate with improved learning outcomes, and usage concentrated around deadlines. How educators contextualised AI use affected learning more than how the tool behaved. I argue that this offloading is partly a product of over-assessment, and that formative, lower-stakes work remains essential precisely because it is where students can afford the desirable difficulties that learning requires. Reducing assessment load is a validity measure, not a soft option. I close with practical starting points for educators, framed around the pedagogical roles AI can play and the risks each carries, and the educator’s role as designer.

Cet article examine comment l’intelligence artificielle (IA) transforme le contrôle de gestion, selon trois axes : les mécanismes de la transformation, les conditions organisationnelles qui en déterminent l’efficacité et l’évolution du rôle du contrôleur de gestion. Une revue systématique de la littérature conduite selon le protocole PRISMA 2020 a permis de retenir 39 articles issus de Scopus et de Google Scholar, publiés entre 2015 et 2026, analysés au moyen d’une matrice de synthèse et d’une analyse thématique transversale. Les résultats mettent en évidence six mécanismes : l’automatisation, l’analytique augmentée, l’intelligence prédictive, l’aide à la décision, le pilotage en temps réel et l’apprentissage organisationnel. Ils identifient quatre conditions organisationnelles : la qualité et la gouvernance des données, les compétences analytiques et numériques, une culture managériale fondée sur les données et la gouvernance de l’IA. La relation entre IA et performance organisationnelle apparaît indirecte et conditionnelle, le contrôle de gestion jouant vraisemblablement un rôle de médiation qui reste à tester, tandis que le rôle du contrôleur évolue vers l’interprétation, l’anticipation et l’aide à la décision. L’article formalise ces résultats dans un modèle intégrateur assorti de six propositions de recherche et propose un agenda de recherche.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The promise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education has motivated a rapidly growing literature whose titles, abstracts, and keywords mention acceptance, attitudes, intention, or perception more than six times as often as self-regulated learning or metacognition. This critical review argues that research on GenAI in education is repeating the founding mistake of learning analytics, measuring what is easy to count rather than what matters for learning. Building on the COPES model of self-regulated learning, this paper develops the gradual reduction of AI delegation (GRAD) framework, in which GenAI performs, proposes, or prompts at eight task stages. Within GRAD, GenAI can take on operations essential to the learning goal. Such delegation helps rather than replaces learning only when the support fades as learners improve. For claims that GenAI improves learning, the paper proposes four validity criteria, namely unassisted outcomes, process evidence, calibration, and ideally gains that outlast the support.
