documents.abstract: Large language models create an accounting information systems design problem: how should evidence production, professional evaluation, and responsibility be allocated between a model and an accountant? We propose a Cognitive Decomposition for Accounting Judgment (CDAJ) coding scheme crossing four process stages with information-intensive and evaluative demands. An Adaptive Collaboration Protocol (ACP) connects allocation rules to an independent human estimate, source-linked model output, structured verification, and a documented human conclusion. Two separately returned coding forms cover 20 constructed cases. A disclosed primary-only analysis retains unresolved auxiliary response formats. Raw agreement is 19/20 for unitization, 20/20 for stage, and 18/20 for demand. On 14 jointly single, codable cases, nominal Cohen's kappa is 1.000 for stage and 0.752 for I/E/M demand profiles; only 12/20 cases are jointly resolved to I or E. A public-disclosure diagnostic searches 1,406 pages for 18 numeric reference cards from three banks' annual reports. Adding a value/period/unit co-occurrence gate to BM25 with identical query information does not improve designated-origin recovery at ranks one or three: both methods recover 13/18 origins at rank one and 18/18 within three ranks. A post-hoc audit distinguishes page recovery from requested table-cell verification. Synthetic checks examine event ordering and record integrity; Gaussian planning experiments examine a future effectiveness evaluation. A separate source-response audit records adverse or unclear statuses in 16/36 returned records. These bounded findings concern coding repeatability and implementation properties. They do not establish an optimal allocation, a validated taxonomy, or improved professional judgment.

Purpose: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming part of everyday work in many organisations. Employees use AI tools to analyse information, respond to customers, check documents, identify patterns and support decisions. In many situations, AI does not work independently; employees and AI systems work together, a relationship known as human–AI collaboration. This paper reviews selected literature on how human–AI collaboration may influence employee performance, and identifies the factors that may explain why employees benefit from AI in some situations but not in others. Methodology: A narrative review of selected conceptual articles, literature reviews and empirical studies on AI use, human–AI interaction, employee attitudes, trust, job design and work performance was carried out. The studies are organised by theme so that their main contributions can be compared. Findings/Result: The reviewed studies indicate that AI can support work speed, productivity, accuracy and decision-making, particularly when tasks are suitable for AI assistance. However, the benefits are not automatic. Outcomes may depend on task complexity, employee skills, trust in AI, training, job design and the level of human control. The literature also identifies concerns such as job insecurity, over-reliance on AI, reduced motivation and the need to check AI-generated outputs. Originality/Value: The paper highlights the need for further research on how trust in AI and job satisfaction may explain the relationship between human–AI collaboration and employee performance, and how job autonomy may influence this relationship. It offers directions for future research and practical suggestions for organisations.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence has significantly transformed foreign language education, particularly the teaching and learning of academic writing. AI-powered applications such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and other generative AI systems provide learners with opportunities to generate ideas, organize arguments, improve grammatical accuracy, expand vocabulary, and receive immediate feedback. However, the increasing integration of AI into writing instruction raises important questions concerning the relationship between technological assistance and human involvement in the writing process. The present study investigates human–AI collaboration in foreign language writing, focusing on its influence on writing performance, learner autonomy, motivation, critical engagement, and academic integrity. A mixed-methods literature-based research design is adopted to synthesize quantitative findings and qualitative evidence from previous empirical studies. The quantitative component examines reported changes in writing performance and patterns of AI-supported learning, while the qualitative component analyzes students' experiences, perceptions, and challenges associated with human–AI interaction. Previous research indicates that AI-assisted writing can contribute to improvements in grammatical accuracy, vocabulary use, text organization, and writing confidence. Mahapatra (2024) reported significant improvements in academic writing performance following a ChatGPT-supported intervention. Similarly, Polakova and Ivenz (2024) identified positive changes in several dimensions of EFL students' writing after receiving AI-generated feedback. However, existing research also highlights concerns related to excessive dependence, reduced originality, inaccurate suggestions, and academic dishonesty. The findings suggest that effective human–AI collaboration requires a balanced relationship in which artificial intelligence provides linguistic and organizational assistance while learners retain responsibility for critical thinking, content development, and final writing decisions. The study concludes that AI should be integrated as a collaborative educational resource rather than a replacement for human creativity, teacher guidance, and independent language development.

This study aimed to determine the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools on learners’ critical thinking and academic performance as a basis for developing an AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit for San Carlos Elementary School, Caba, La Union. Specifically, it examined learners’ awareness and experiences in using AI tools, their level of critical thinking, academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English, and the relationship among these variables. The study employed a quantitative research design involving twenty-six (26) learner-respondents who answered a validated and reliable survey questionnaire. The findings revealed that learners had a high level of awareness of AI tools, including ChatGPT, Grammarly, QuillBot, and Jenni AI, while their learning and collaborative experiences were very high. Their overall level of critical thinking was high, with a median of 4.17, particularly in reasoning, problem-solving, and collaborative skills. Likewise, their academic performance in Mathematics, Science, and English was very high, with grades ranging from 91 to 95. Statistical analysis further revealed a significant but weak positive correlation between awareness of AI tools and critical thinking (r = .300), as well as a significant positive correlation with academic performance in Mathematics (r = .343). These findings suggest that AI tools can support learners’ critical thinking and academic performance when integrated meaningfully and responsibly into instruction. The developed AI-Driven Instructional Toolkit obtained a very high level of validity, indicating its suitability for instructional use. The study recommends the guided integration of AI tools to promote responsible technology use, independent thinking, collaborative learning, and improved academic outcomes.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The Industry 4.0 era demands a transformation of electrical engineering higher education so that graduates meet modern industry needs. This article examines the forms of digital technology used in electrical engineering learning, their impact on learning outcomes, implementation challenges, and optimization strategies. A systematic literature review was conducted on 32 peer-reviewed articles published from 2020 to 2024, selected from 142 records across five international academic databases. Thematic analysis identified five technology categories: software-based simulation, virtual laboratories, the Internet of Things, learning management system-based online learning, and artificial intelligence for personalized learning. Virtual laboratories showed a significant effect on learning outcomes, with the largest effects on motivation and student engagement. Implementation faces challenges including variation in lecturers' digital competence, limited infrastructure, resistance to change, and accessibility for students with disabilities. Recommended strategies include integrated blended learning, continuing engineering education for lecturers, cloud computing investment, industry–academia collaboration, and universal design principles. Successful integration requires a holistic approach supported by institutional commitment and a shift in stakeholder mindsets.

This paper presents key insights from the AIthena project on trust-worthy and human-centric artificial intelligence (AI) to support large-scale deployment of Connected, Cooperative and Automated Mobility (CCAM) systems. It explores how AI can enhance perception, situational awareness and trans-parent decision-making to enable safe, explainable and context-sensitive automation. By addressing challenges across vehicle, mobility system and industrial level, the paper identifies technological and systemic enablers for a re-liable adoption. At the vehicle level, the project identifies critical weaknesses in current AI solutions, proposing enhancements through Explainable AI (XAI) to improve robustness and transparency across perception, scenario understanding and decision-making. It also addresses development challenges, including realistic data collection, complex testing and detailed reporting to meet transparency requirements. At mobility level, the project tackles AI trustworthiness in complex, mixed-traffic environments. It proposes methods to evaluate the reliability of V2X data and supports adaptive routing through AI-based reasoning models that integrate sensor data and behavioural context. At the industry level, the paper examines enablers such as standard alignment, regulatory frameworks and innovation ecosystem maturity. A preliminary roadmap is proposed for deploying explainable and accountable AI in CCAM, aiming to align technology, governance and user expectations to-wards sustainable, inclusive mobility in Europe.

La proliferación de la desinformación digital impulsa el uso de sistemas de inteligencia artificial (IA) en la verificación informativa. Este estudio analiza el rendimiento técnico de estas herramientas y la confianza ciudadana en su aplicación al fact-checking. Con diseño mixto, se examinan 150 informes de verificación que integran IA y una encuesta a 600 usuarios de redes sociales de España y América Latina. Los resultados muestran elevada eficacia en la verificación automatizada y una confianza moderada, condicionada por la transparencia algorítmica y los sesgos. Se concluye que los modelos híbridos IA-humanos constituyen la estrategia más sólida para la verificación informativa.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Humanity faces interconnected planetary challenges, including climate change, biodiversity loss, food and water insecurity, public health crises, and persistent inequality. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has shown strong potential to address such problems, yet AI used in isolation can be opaque, biased, energy-intensive, and detached from the ecological and human contexts it is meant to serve. This paper introduces the International Society for Artificial Intelligence and Real Intelligence (ISAIRI), a proposed global society dedicated to making the Earth a better place to live through a new interdisciplinary field called AIRI. AIRI is defined as the field that solves problems of the Earth using both Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Real Intelligence (RI). In this paper, RI is taken to mean Natural Intelligence; this is the current working definition and will be refined in future publications. We present the motivation, definitions, guiding principles, an operational framework, priority domains, an organizational model, and a phased roadmap for ISAIRI, and we discuss open challenges and directions for future work.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into environmental, economic, and social decision-making processes raises ethical questions about AI systems. To address such questions, this study investigates the relationships of AI systems with anthropocentrism, ecocentrism, and biocentrism. The study also examines the moderating role of ethical governance on these relationships. Environmental ethics theory, systems theory, institutional theory, and technological determinism theory provide the foundation for the theoretical framework. The study employs quantitative methodology and a positivist philosophy. A structured survey was used for data collection, using questionnaires adopted from previous studies. The population includes university teachers with AI expertise and environmental knowledge, and the sample size is 410. Partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used for the analysis of the data. The findings reveal that AI systems have positive and significant relationships with anthropocentrism, ecocentrism, and biocentrism. The results also show that ethical governance moderates the relationships between AI systems and between anthropocentrism and ecocentrism. Surprisingly, it does not show a moderating role in the relationship between AI systems and biocentrism. Importantly, differences in the strength of these relationships exist. Furthermore, the study highlights the importance of ethical governance in shaping AI systems decisions. This study extends the current discussion of AI systems and environmental ethics and provides theoretical, practical, and managerial implications for researchers, AI developers, and users by integrating ethical orientations into the development priorities of AI and environmental responsibility.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Plenty of students now ask AI to explain a topic, check an essay, or settle a decision. But does depending on AI for tasks like these also tie them to it emotionally? This study looked at whether reliance on AI predicts Human–AI relationship among university students. We used a cross-sectional survey design and collected data from 300 students (158 men, 142 women) through convenient sampling. Reliance was measured with the Reliance on Artificial Intelligence Scale (RAI-15; Yap et al., 2023) and the Human–AI relationship with the Experiences in Human–AI Relationships Scale (EHARS; Yang & Oshio, 2025). Reliability was acceptable to good (α = .76 and .83). Reliance on AI was positively correlated with Human–AI relationship (r = .23, p < .001) and was a significant but modest predictor of it, explaining about 5% of the variance. Men reported higher reliance on AI (d = 0.32) and a stronger Human–AI relationship (d = 0.34) than women. The results suggest that using and depending on AI for practical purposes is linked to an emotional bond with it, though only weakly. We discuss what this means for AI literacy and for future research in Pakistan.

Interpreting the predictions of complex black-box classifiers remains a central challenge in explainable artificial intelligence. While local explanations clarify individual predictions, there is a significant need for global probabilistic explanations that capture a model's overall behavior across the input distribution. Such an explanation is a small subset $K$ of features, whose relevance is measured by the expected probability, over a random input $\mathbf x$, that the classifier assigns the same label to $\mathbf x$ and to a random input agreeing with $\mathbf x$ on $K$. In this study, we investigate the task of identifying maximally relevant global explanations under a cardinality constraint, focusing on product distributions with full support on discrete feature spaces. We introduce a spectral explainer that leverages membership queries to the black-box classifier and employs Fourier-analytic, junta-learning methods to produce probably approximately correct (PAC) explanations. Our algorithm is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to the explanation size limit, maximum feature cardinality, and desired accuracy. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm the theoretical guarantees and show that the spectral explainer outperforms a greedy baseline as the explanation size increases.

Conversation with generative artificial intelligence (AI) can quickly turn a tentative scientific question into the outline of a research programme. Although this capability can accelerate research, it also places two closely related pressures on human intelligence: 1) temporal asymmetry between rapid AI generation and slower expert evaluation, and 2) a cognitive gap between the available effort, expertise, attention and capacity to assess AI outputs. When unexamined AI contributions are carried into subsequent claims or decisions, these pressures produce verification debt: validation work that remains outstanding before a contribution can be relied upon. If left unresolved, this debt can undermine responsible AI in research, understood here as the transparent and traceable use of AI under effective human oversight and accountability. This commentary argues that responsible human--AI research partnerships therefore require a disciplined method for managing verification debt, not better prompting alone. We propose a shared topology of the research programme: a structured representation that connects questions, claims, assumptions, sources, tests and decisions while recording their provenance, dependencies and verification status. The topology makes unresolved debt visible, enables corrections to propagate through dependent claims and requires consequential contributions to be examined at decision gates before research proceeds. We consider its application in two-way partnerships and supervised partnerships that extend from doctoral research to multi-way research teams, and examine its implications for scholarly assessment, peer review and empirical evaluation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human performance in the performing arts is a complex, multifaceted experience intertwining technical proficiency, artistic expression, and psychological resilience to anxiety and stress. One key factor influencing a musician’s success and well-being is self-perceived performance quality (SPPQ), which plays a vital role in motivation, confidence, and career longevity. Sport psychology frameworks such as S.F.E.R.A. (Synchrony, Force/Strength, Energy, Rhythm, Activation) support optimal performance by monitoring and improving related mental factors. This study investigated the relationships among SPPQ, music performance anxiety (MPA), and mental skills as assessed by the SFERA model in professional musicians. Eighty-two participants (53% females) completed an online survey including the SFERA questionnaire and the Kenny Music Performance Anxiety Inventory (K-MPAI). We found significant negative correlations between SPPQ and MPA, and significant positive correlations between SPPQ and SFERA (total and subfactor scores). “Force” (i.e., strength of personal resources), proximal somatic anxiety, memory issues, and biological vulnerability emerged as the strongest predictors of SPPQ in the variable importance analysis. In other words, musicians with higher anxiety tended to report lower SPPQ and lower SFERA mental skills. Further mediation analysis showed that SFERA scores mediated approximately 60% (proportion mediated = 0.618, 95% confidence interval [0.148, 1.331]) of the association between MPA and SPPQ. These findings underscore the applicability of sport-based mental skills models to music contexts and highlight the potential protective role of mental skills in mitigating the impact of performance anxiety on performers’ self-perceived quality.

In recent years, the increased use of biodegradable materials has raised several concerns regarding their flammability and thermal reactivity when exposed to intense heat radiation from nearby fires. Among others, Poly(lactic acid) (PLA) is one of the most commercially successful biodegradable polymers in several applications and industrial sectors such as packaging, consumer goods, and automotive components. This work presents a multi-scale experimental investigation of PLA degradation, combining small-scale analyses (i.e., thermogravimetric analysis coupled with FTIR and mass spectrometry) with bench-scale testing (i.e., cone calorimetry). The integration of these techniques, supported by temperature distribution measurements, enables the identification of the sequential physical and chemical phenomena controlling ignition, volatilisation, and combustion, providing a comprehensive evaluation of the fire response of the material across different conditions. Small scale tests have identified a decomposition temperature of ∼250 °C either in nitrogen or air, indicating a limited contribution of heterogeneous reactions within the decomposition process. At bench scale, a threshold value of 15 kW/m 2 was identified as the maximum external heat flux to guarantee the absence of sustained ignition or self-sustained decomposition. The formation of acetic acid was identified as a key intermediate, with apparent flame spread velocities (S u,app ) ranging from 0.0011 to 0.0018 cm/s, indicating gas-phase reactions occur almost instantaneously once volatiles are released. The characteristic times of the key thermal phenomena were quantified through combined analysis of heat release profiles, evolved gases, and temperature gradients, revealing that the temporal evolution of melting, liquid heating, and volatilisation occurs over comparable time scales. This approach advances the mechanistic understanding of bio-based polymer combustion and provides valuable tools for the design of safer materials in fire-sensitive industrial applications.

Burnout syndrome is an important occupational health issue associated with working conditions and work organization. This study aimed to report an educational intervention focused on raising awareness about burnout and promoting mental health among workers. This is a descriptive experience report carried out with employees of an occupational health and safety company. Active participation by the workers was observed, encouraging discussions on psychosocial risk factors, burnout prevention, and self-care. It is concluded that educational actions are a complementary strategy for promoting mental health and strengthening a preventive culture within organizations, in accordance with the guidelines of NR-1.

Quality of Working Life (QWL) is an important dimension of mental health promotion in organizations. This study aimed to report and analyze an extension experience focused on promoting QWL in an occupational health and safety company in Praia Grande, São Paulo, Brazil. This qualitative and descriptive experience report was conducted by Psychology students through a dialogic lecture with 12 employees. Active participation and reports concerning time management, internal communication, and occupational stress were observed. The experience encouraged reflection on mental health and the integration of theory and practice, indicating the relevance of psychoeducational actions in organizational contexts.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: In this study, we adopted a holistic approach by integrating bibliometric analysis and systematic review methods to thoroughly evaluate the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in mathematics education and its research trends. The study aims to understand the current state of the field and provide strategic direction for future research by assessing general trends, intellectual contributions, and application potential in AI-focused mathematics education research from a multidimensional perspective. In the first phase, we conducted a content analysis of 363 articles published in high-quality journals indexed in the Web of Science (WoS) database, focusing on dimensions such as publishers, method types, research designs, study groups, theoretical or conceptual frameworks, data collection techniques, preferred technologies, purposes of use, and roles. Subsequently, we conducted a comprehensive and systematic evaluation of scientific productivity, citation performance, collaboration networks, conceptual structures, thematic maps, and intellectual transformations. During this process, we followed the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA). The findings indicate that AI technologies have been increasingly utilized in mathematics education, with significant growth observed since 2015. AI-focused mathematics education research has been predominantly concentrated in countries like the USA, China, and Germany, delving into areas such as personalized learning, assessment, feedback, and pedagogical innovations. Most studies have employed quantitative and mixed methods, with middle school and undergraduate students being the primary target groups. Bibliometric analyses reveal a rapid expansion in scientific productivity and collaboration networks, while thematic trends primarily focus on personalized learning and the integration of digital tools.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Students today do not just use AI tools; many talk to them, confide in them, and sometimes describe them in almost personal terms. This study asked whether the extent to which students perceive AI as human-like (AI anthropomorphism) is linked to the emotional bond they report having with AI (Human–AI relationship). Using a cross-sectional survey design, data were collected from 300 university students (158 men and 142 women) through convenient sampling. Anthropomorphism was assessed with the Scale of AI Anthropomorphism (SAIA; Xu et al., 2026) and the Human–AI relationship with the Experiences in Human–AI Relationships Scale (EHARS; Yang & Oshio, 2025). Reliability was good for both measures (α = .91 and .83). Anthropomorphism and Human–AI relationship were positively correlated (r = .38, p < .001), and anthropomorphism significantly predicted Human–AI relationship, accounting for roughly 14% of its variance. Male students scored higher than female students on both variables, with small effects (d = 0.28 and 0.34). Students who see more of a "mind" in AI therefore tend to report stronger attachment-related experiences with it. The implications for AI literacy, responsible technology use, and future research in Pakistan are discussed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

This article discusses the key stages of integrating digital technologies and artificial intelligence into foreign language teaching. Going beyond the standard four-stage SAMR transformation model, the author analyzes key pedagogical dimensions, including learner autonomy, multi-layered cognitive AI roles, and human-AI co-agency. Practical aspects of technology implementation and adaptive learning ecosystems are highlighted.

This systematic analytical review examines technology prioritisation patterns in construction safety technology (CST) research and how injury-burden evidence is reported and used in study rationales and evaluations. It distinguishes the documented use of injury-consequence evidence from the safety relevance of the hazards addressed and from demonstrated reductions in harm. A review of 148 peer-reviewed CST studies published between 2016, and April 2026 was conducted using Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect. Studies were coded across eight domains covering safety functions, risk contexts, data and intelligence characteristics, human–technology interaction, adoption maturity, system architecture, evaluation approaches, and burden considerations. Methodological quality was appraised using the Quality Assessment Tool for Studies with Diverse Designs (QATSDD), and threshold- and quality-stratified sensitivity analyses tested the robustness of the synthesis. The review introduces the Technology Prioritisation Logic Framework as an analytical construct for organising recurring study characteristics, together with an assessment of reported burden integration in problem framing and evaluation. Findings show that CST research is concentrated around prevention, detection/monitoring, computer vision, wearable sensing, machine learning, alerts, and managerial reporting, while severity, time loss, cost, and long-term worker impact remain weakly integrated. The findings support a shift toward burden-informed safety technology design, evaluation, and governance.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is changing the economics and operational speed of cyberattacks. The growing ability of AI systems and autonomous agents to investigate targets, generate attack strategies, coordinate operations and execute successive actions creates a challenge for conventional security architectures. The critical issue is not necessarily a single malicious operation. It is the possibility of asequence of individually plausible actions that collectively produces an unauthorized result. This paper proposes a defensive architectural response combining ST-T1024, theDeterministic Trust and Authorization Layer (DTAL), and the A1–A17 agentic researchframework. The proposal separates intelligence from operational authority. An AI agent may investigate, reason, identify weaknesses and propose actions. However, its ability to execute actions remains subject to identity, authorization, information-graph relationships, link-specific costs, budgets and explicit thresholds. DTAL provides a mechanism for evaluating successive actions against an organization'sauthorization structure. ST-T1024 provides the proposed deterministic foundation for bounded decision processes. A1–A17 contribute complementary mechanisms for bounded agency, verification and behavioural analysis. The central defensive principle is straightforward:When an action sequence violates an established authorization boundary, furtherexecution must be stopped. The paper develops this proposition through illustrative attack scenarios, identifies theconditions required for effectiveness, and proposes a path toward independent validation. It does not claim that the architecture has already been experimentally proven to prevent all cyberattacks.

INTRODUCTION: Perceived parental autonomy support plays a central role in fostering adolescents' academic engagement, yet little research has simultaneously examined its bidirectional associations with academic engagement or the mechanisms explaining these links. To address this gap, this study used cross-lagged panel modeling (CLPM) and random-intercept cross-lagged panel modeling (RI-CLPM) to investigate reciprocal relationships among perceived parental autonomy support, subjective intergenerational mobility, and academic engagement, while testing the mediating role of subjective intergenerational mobility. METHODS: Participants were 738 Chinese adolescents (55.9% male; Mage = 14.58 years, SD = 0.59) who completed three waves of data collection at 6-month intervals. RESULTS: Results from the CLPM indicated reciprocal associations between perceived parental autonomy support and subjective intergenerational mobility. In contrast, the RI-CLPM revealed a more differentiated dynamic pattern: perceived parental autonomy support at T1 predicted subjective intergenerational mobility at T2, which subsequently predicted perceived parental autonomy support at T3. Furthermore, subjective intergenerational mobility predicted academic engagement only in the CLPM but not in the RI-CLPM. Importantly, both modeling approaches consistently demonstrated a stable reciprocal association between perceived parental autonomy support and academic engagement. CONCLUSION: These findings highlight the importance of considering temporal dynamics and individual differences when examining the relationships among perceived parental autonomy support, subjective intergenerational mobility, and adolescents' academic engagement. The results suggest that enhancing perceived parental autonomy support and strengthening adolescents' perceptions of intergenerational mobility may serve as vital pathways to sustain and promote long-term academic engagement.

documents.abstract: This essay challenges the idea that P vs NP adequately represents the broader limits of human and computational problem-solving. While recognizing its mathematical validity, it argues that real-world solvability depends on more than polynomial-time algorithms—including accumulated knowledge, evolving computational systems, artificial intelligence, collaboration, and physical constraints. Rather than claiming to solve P vs NP, the paper questions whether its prominence among the Millennium Prize Problems still reflects the deeper questions we should be asking about computation, intelligence, and the nature of solvability.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence has significantly transformed English as a Foreign Language (EFL) academic writing practices. AI-powered applications, particularly ChatGPT, provide students with opportunities to generate ideas, organize arguments, receive feedback, improve grammatical accuracy, and revise academic texts. However, the increasing use of these technologies has raised important questions concerning their relationship with students' critical thinking abilities. The present study examines the relationship between AI use and critical thinking in EFL academic writing, focusing on analytical reasoning, evaluation of information, argument development, independent decision-making, and reflective writing practices. A qualitative, literature-based research design is adopted to investigate how AI-assisted writing influences students' cognitive engagement and academic performance. Previous research suggests that structured AI-assisted instruction can support critical thinking when students actively evaluate generated information, question suggestions, and make independent decisions. At the same time, excessive dependence on AI-generated content may reduce opportunities for independent reasoning and original idea development. Recent empirical studies involving EFL university students have demonstrated positive associations between guided ChatGPT use, critical thinking, and writing proficiency. The study emphasizes that the educational value of AI depends not simply on the frequency of its use but on the quality of students' interaction with the technology. It concludes that AI should function as a supportive learning resource rather than a replacement for human reasoning. Integrating critical thinking activities into AI-assisted academic writing instruction may help EFL students develop stronger analytical, evaluative, and independent writing abilities.

documents.abstract: Motivation is a mental construct present in academic, social, and family settings. The objective of this research was to analyze the relationship and fit a regression line between Intrinsic Motivation to Accomplish (independent variable x) and Intrinsic Motivation to Experience Stimulation (dependent variable y). A total of 116 university students participated in the study. Data were collected using the Academic Motivation Scale (AMS), developed by Vallerand et al. (1989). A non-experimental, correlational design was followed. A significance level of alpha = 0.05 was adopted. A significant positive Pearson correlation (r = 0.69; p < 0.05) was found between the variables. A linear regression line of y = 0.6504x + 2.6641 was determined.

Voice systems increasingly combine streaming speech, persistent state, reasoning, tool use, and embodied control. Once these functions share a runtime, spoken input can change digital or physical state, and recognition or response quality alone no longer characterizes the system. This article studies the interfaces through which spoken evidence becomes consequential. \emph{Auditory intelligence} denotes the capabilities required to perceive, understand, coordinate, and generate spoken interaction; \emph{auditory agency} denotes the causal path from that interaction to stateful decisions and observable consequences. The \emph{commitment boundary} marks where revisable auditory evidence becomes persistent state, a plan, or an executable request. \emph{Agency closure} then follows an authorized action through observation, verification, recovery or compensation, and communication of the outcome. Evidence from full-duplex interaction, reasoning, memory, tools, embodiment, and human control shows a consistent systems-level mismatch: integration is advancing faster than end-to-end observation of what the integrated system actually does. The resulting design problem is to preserve a trace from spoken evidence to consequence while keeping commitment, execution, and verification attributable.

Artificial intelligence increasingly supports the interpretation, prioritisation and presentation of information in high-stakes organisational settings. Yet the formal presence of a human decision-maker does not establish effective human control. This working paper develops a socio-technical and normative perspective on human oversight in AI-supported situation assessment, with particular attention to governmental security analysis and critical electric power infrastructure in Austria and Germany. Drawing selectively on Heidegger, Schelsky and Latour, it examines how technical systems structure what becomes visible, actionable and contestable. Kant’s ideas of public justification and Jonas’s ethics of responsibility provide a normative orientation, while Ben Green’s critique of individual human oversight highlights the importance of institutional governance. Drawing on Vaughan and Elish, the paper argues that institutional oversight depends in part on organised capacities for contestation by professionals. Four analytical dimensions are proposed: epistemic pre-structuring, practical verifiability, the capacity to contest system outputs, and the attribution of responsibility. Existing empirical research in security operations centres and electricity control rooms demonstrates that the subject is already under investigation, and raises questions for comparative research. The paper also outlines a future qualitative study based on expert interviews. Its central proposition is that meaningful oversight must be studied as an organisational capability, not merely as an individual duty.

documents.abstract: Partially automated driving (PAD) systems are becoming increasingly prevalent in consumer vehicles. While drivers are obliged to monitor the roadway and the system during PAD, they do not always comply with this requirement and may engage in non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs). Literature has emphasized the detrimental effects of visual-manual NDRTs on drivers' capability to takeover control from PAD while reporting negligible effects of non-visual NDRTs (e.g., hands-free phone calls) and cognitive load. However, most studies focused on alerted scenarios, with takeover requests lowering drivers' reliance on anticipation and cognitive control, masking the effects of cognitive load. Related work also examined PAD conditions alone, neglecting the combined effects of automation and cognitive load on drivers' responses. To address the gaps, we conducted a driving simulator study examining the influence of cognitive load, induced by a 2-back task, on driver-initiated responses to urban traffic hazards (e.g., crossing pedestrians, oncoming vehicles) during both manual driving and PAD. The timing and quality of driver-initiated responses were analysed separately for each hazard with detail. Results showed that driver-initiated responses during PAD were less anticipatory and relied more on cognitive control. This shift led to higher situational criticality and heightened susceptibility of responses to cognitive load during PAD. Hazard characteristics such as motion speed and cue ambiguity appeared to influence cognitive load effects and warrant systematic examination in future work. Together, these findings underscore an elevated safety risk associated with cognitive load during PAD, especially in scenarios requiring cognitively demanding, driver-initiated intervention.

Human oversight in AI-assisted decision-making is often examined from the moment a person receives a recommendation. Yet the information, alternatives and conditions available to that person may already have been shaped by earlier technical and institutional choices. Drawing on established research in organisational decision theory, agenda-setting power, system-level bureaucracy, technological due process and sociotechnical accountability, this working paper examines a question at their intersection: who governs the conditions under which a human–AI decision becomes possible, and who can legitimately examine or reconsider those conditions? The paper explores the relationship between authority over institutional decisions and authority over their formation, considering how responsibilities and effective oversight capabilities may be distributed across organisations and affected by subsequent changes. It situates this discussion within existing European AI governance and data-protection law. Its proposed contribution is integrative rather than a claim of originality for the individual concepts involved. The paper does not presume that additional external authorisation is necessary, nor does it claim empirical validation of the proposed analytical perspective. Published within ID∆AC Research as a public discussion working paper, this contribution invites critical engagement from researchers and practitioners in law, organisational theory, AI governance, sociotechnical systems and institutional accountability. Comments, counterarguments, overlooked intellectual precedents and alternative institutional interpretations are particularly welcome. The purpose is to refine the question through informed disagreement and interdisciplinary exchange. Empirical validation remains open.

documents.abstract: This academic article aims to examine and analyze the systematic relationship between leadership and the creation of Employee Engagement, which is considered a strategic variable directly affecting organizational performance and sustainability within the context of today’s socio-economic environment. Through content analysis of instructional documents and contemporary research studies, the literature review reveals that Employee Engagement is a significant variable reflecting employees’ psychological characteristics, including commitment, dedication, and willingness to perform at their full potential. These characteristics demonstrate a statistically significant positive relationship with organizational performance. Furthermore, the study found that leadership, particularly Transformational Leadership and Servant Leadership, plays a causal role in enhancing engagement levels through several mechanisms, including the creation of intrinsic motivation, emotional and psychological support, effective organizational communication, and the cultivation of meaningfulness in work. In addition, contextual factors such as organizational culture and human resource management policies serve as supporting variables that strengthen and sustain engagement levels over time. Organizations that maintain a positive working environment are more capable of managing engagement effectively. This article also proposes the Leadership–Engagement Integration Model as a new body of knowledge that can be applied in digital-era organizations. The model emphasizes the development of leaders through Agile Leadership alongside the application of technology and data analytics to measure and analyze engagement levels concretely. In conclusion, leadership is regarded as a strategic factor with significant implications for the development of Employee Engagement and serves as a fundamental foundation for long-term organizational success.

This paper addresses the ongoing debate on whether AI helps accelerate developments in the field of Mathematics or does it come at a greater cost. It explores the very principles and foundations that have guided mathematicians for centuries in the context of today’s issue. It then examines the tension between accelerating mathematical discovery through automated proof generation and preserving human intuition, verification, and intellectual rigor. The paper does not seek to dismiss the organizations involved in building the artificial intelligence tools, rather it aims to advocate for a balanced approach where these technologies can be sustainably integrated into mathematical working, rather than completely replacing human intuition and rigour.

Objective: To understand the perception and level of knowledge of nursing students regarding the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in healthcare services. Methods: This was an exploratory-descriptive, cross-sectional and quantitative study, conducted with 302 students from two educational institutions in Altamira, Pará. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire addressing perceived usefulness, ease of use from the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and ethical dilemmas. The analysis occurred via descriptive statistics using Microsoft Excel® software. The study was approved by a Research Ethics Committee. Results: The sample presented a female majority (75.8%) and brown skin color (60.6%). The "Invisibility Paradox" phenomenon was found: although 81.5% affirmed prior contact with AI, 46.4% failed to recognize its clinical applications, and 56.6% judged their knowledge as basic. Through the TAM model, utility (time optimization and diagnostic support) is recognized, but the need for extensive training acts as a barrier. Ethically, decision opacity and the replacement of clinical judgment (totally feared by 40.7%) are the greatest challenges. Conclusion: It is concluded that AI integration is accepted by students as clinical support, provided it preserves the autonomy of the augmented nurse and humanized care.

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important technological advancement in the field of education. It supports students through personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems, automated assessments, and virtual academic assistance. The use of Artificial Intelligence helps students improve their learning efficiency, understanding of subjects, and overall academic performance. This study aims to analyse the role of Artificial Intelligence in enhancing academic performance among students. The study focuses on students’ awareness, usage, and perception of AI-based educational tools. Primary data were collected through a structured questionnaire, and secondary data were collected from journals, books, and research articles. The study reveals that Artificial Intelligence has a positive influence on students’ academic performance, though challenges such as lack of awareness and technical skills still exist. Suitable suggestions are provided to improve the effective use of Artificial Intelligence in the academic environment.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming higher education worldwide, reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, student support, and institutional governance. Recent systematic reviews show a rapid growth of AI applications in higher education but highlight persistent gaps in ethics, evidence, and policy coherence. In the Arab region, AI adoption is unfolding within ambitious national digital transformation agendas, including UAE’s National Strategy for AI 2031, Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030, and Oman Vision 2040, which explicitly position AI as a strategic lever for human capital development and economic diversification. Arab universities are experimenting with generative AI in teaching and student support, deploying chatbots, analytics, and AI-enabled curricula, while grappling with issues of academic integrity, equity, and institutional readiness. This article synthesizes global and regional evidence on AI in higher education, with particular attention to generative AI and its implications for the Arab region. It proposes the Strategic AI in Higher Education (SAIHE) framework, designed as a practical guide for institutional leaders. The framework integrates five domains Vision and Strategy; Governance, Ethics and Risk; Teaching, Learning and Assessment; Student Success and Experience; and Capacity, Culture and Infrastructure underpinned by a cross-cutting layer of evidence and continuous improvement. The article concludes by outlining implications for institutional leaders, quality assurance bodies, and policymakers, and identifies directions for future research on AI-enabled transformation in Arab higher education systems.

documents.abstract: This study examined the individual and joint associations of AI-driven strategic leadership and artificial intelligence (AI) adoption with perceived organisational adaptability among private organisations in Accra, Ghana. A quantitative-priority mixed-methods, descriptive-correlational design combined questionnaires from 799 respondents (399 leaders and 400 employees) in 84 organisations with 25 key-informant interviews. Random-intercept multilevel regression assessed leadership and adoption while adjusting for respondent category, organisation size, tenure and sector; supplementary models and thematic analysis examined robustness and context. Organisation-level clustering was meaningful (intraclass correlations = .240-.414). Adding AI-driven strategic leadership to the controls model was associated with greater perceived adaptability (B = 0.577, 95% CI [0.511, 0.643], p< .001), increasing marginal R² from .210 to .428. In the joint model, leadership remained the larger correlate (B = 0.494, p< .001), while adoption contributed a smaller independent association (B = 0.153, p< .001); marginal R² reached .448. Respondent-category interactions were not significant. None of seven exploratory leadership dimensions remained individually significant after Holm adjustment. Findings support the relevance of integrated leadership practices beyond reported AI access, but the cross-sectional self-report design does not establish causality. Organisations should combine documented AI direction, workforce preparation, governance and objective monitoring of adaptation.

documents.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to support students during learning and problem solving, but its instructional value depends on how it is embedded in established learning approaches. Worked examples guide learners through the steps and reasoning of a solution; conversational AI may extend them by responding to individual questions. To isolate this added value, we compared a chatbot-delivered intelligent worked example with a matched static worked example and a lecture script. Nine recitation groups in an undergraduate electrodynamics course were cluster-randomized to the three conditions, and 86 students worked individually on a Gauss's law problem. Concept-test accuracy and self-efficacy increased significantly in all conditions, but changes did not differ significantly between groups (p=.07 for concept-test accuracy and p=.38 for self-efficacy). Four weeks later, in a reduced sample with selective participation and pre-existing group differences, students in the static worked-example condition scored higher than those in the script condition (p=.004, d=1.22), whereas the two worked-example conditions did not differ significantly. Usability, but not perceived educational value, was higher for the intelligent worked example than for the script (p=.011, d=0.88). In a subsequent homework assignment on Ampere's law with free choice of learning material (N=46), 62-71% of students in each condition reported using only the static worked example, at most 8% used exclusively the intelligent one, and 15-31% used neither. Thus, conversational delivery showed no clear additional learning benefit under the present conditions. More broadly, a learning format that is rated favorably need not be the one students voluntarily adopt.

documents.abstract: How can employee groups influence identity regulation within their organisation? While recognising that employees have agency in their response to organisational identity control, the literature has largely positioned identity regulation as a managerial prerogative enforced through disciplinary power. Some research, however, finds that groups of employees are able to shape their members’ identities and oppose or negotiate managerial attempts to influence them. This article extends the identity regulation research by showing how employee groups can go beyond merely reacting to managerial identity regulation; they can also appropriate and redirect it to influence other employees. Using an in-depth case study, we analyse how an environmental insider activist group managed to do so through two interrelated tactics: augmenting the ideal employee identity built and promoted by management and repurposing existing identity regulation practices and discourses. By demonstrating how employee groups without disciplinary power can appropriate and transform managerial identity regulation for a cause they care about, these findings contribute to knowledge on identity regulation dynamics within organisations and on the relationships between identity regulation and broader societal norms.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is considered as a field of computer science dedicated to creating an integrated machine capable of performing tasks that systematically requires human intelligence such as learning, reasoning, decision or problem-solving. It also refers to the simulation of human intelligence in machines that are programmed to think, learn, and make decisions like humans (ADETUTU, 2026) objectives: This issue aims to propose new ways of looking at education systems in terms of content, evaluation and assessments, pedagogy, the role of the teacher, and capturing and integrating voices of the youth in education systems. Curriculum development at the basic education is a foundational standard for greater advancement in Multicultural paradigm. The current focus has shifted from "using tech" to "integrating intelligence" that supports both the teacher and the learner. Recommendations: Integrating AI into classroom assessment offers the potential to enhance efficiency, objectivity, and pedagogical decision-making. The following assertions are made to have a robust foundational AI education in the country: Pilot Testing & Capacity Building Professional Development (TPD): Implement continuous, hands-on training for primary school teachers focusing on facilitation techniques, cross-curricular planning, and formative assessment. Conclusion: AI usage has emerged as an integral part of several sectors, altering the way businesses and personnel engage with technology. The rapid evolution of artificial intelligence within educational contexts presents significant opportunities for refining classroom assessment methodologies through the deployment o AI-driven instruments (Ayo, 2025).

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teachers’ instructional planning, learning design, assessment, feedback, and professional work. This study examined whether teachers’ AI literacy predicts pedagogical innovation and technology integration among the 68 permanent teachers of Maydolong National High School, Maydolong District, Eastern Samar. A quantitative, non-experimental predictive-correlational design was used, with total population sampling. Data were gathered through an adapted questionnaire measuring AI literacy, pedagogical innovation, technology integration, technology access, AI experience, and AI-related training. The findings showed very high AI literacy (M = 4.587, SD = 0.409), very high pedagogical innovation (M = 4.423, SD = 0.490), and very high frequency of technology integration (M = 4.366, SD = 0.462). Critical Evaluation of AI was the highest AI-literacy dimension (M = 4.728), while AI for Professional Learning was the lowest, although still very high (M = 4.403). Pearson correlation revealed a strong positive relationship between AI literacy and pedagogical innovation (r = .685, p < .001), but a negligible and non-significant relationship between AI literacy and general technology integration (r = -.009, p = .940). Simple linear regression showed that AI literacy significantly predicted pedagogical innovation, explaining 47.0% of its variance (β = .685, R² = .470, p < .001), but did not predict technology integration (β = -.009, R² ≈ .000, p = .940). The findings indicate that AI literacy is particularly relevant to pedagogical innovation, whereas broader technology integration is likely shaped by additional contextual factors such as infrastructure, access, professional development, and institutional support.

Digitalization and artificial intelligence (AI) can expand access, productivity, and service delivery in developing countries, yet their benefits are distributed unevenly and may reinforce pre-existing structural inequalities. This systematic review distinguishes foundational digitalization from more computationally intensive AI applications and re-audits the evidence base in response to concerns about scope and reproducibility. Of the 75 publications retained in the broader literature corpus, 57 meet the prespecified criteria for the systematic synthesis; 18 are retained only as contextual/background literature and are not included in evidence counts. The review uses PRISMA 2020 reporting principles and a design-specific Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) procedure for eligible empirical studies. The thematic synthesis presents four interconnected mechanisms: unequal digital and AI capabilities, workforce and value-distribution pressures, uneven socio-economic results, and governance constraints. These are integrated into the ‘Vicious Cycle of Techno-Dependency’ as an interpretive framework, not a tested causal model. Evidence indicates that the strength and form of these mechanisms vary across country contexts and institutional capacities. Recent post-search studies from Brazil, India, and Indonesia further suggest that data-protection and sovereignty initiatives can strengthen accountability, but their effectiveness is conditional and remains incomplete. Policy priorities therefore include locally appropriate infrastructure and skills investment, participatory data governance, algorithmic accountability, and evaluation of implementation outcomes rather than reliance on formal policy adoption alone.
